incisive

in-SY-siv · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Incisive is sharply clear and precise in thought or expression; cutting straight to the heart of a matter.

The young analyst's incisive comment during the meeting impressed everyone on the board, cutting through hours of vague discussion in a single sentence.

Example

In one incisive paragraph, the editor managed to summarize the entire four-hundred-page book's central conflict.

Incisive praises precision and clarity of thought -- it doesn't necessarily criticize or wound anyone, unlike a harsher, more cutting word.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sharp: A sharp mind or remark is quick and acute -- it catches what others miss and answers fast. Incisive adds depth and aim: an incisive comment does not just react quickly; it cuts straight to what actually matters and lays it bare. Many sharp remarks are merely clever; an incisive one settles the question.

penetrating: Penetrating describes insight that gets beneath the surface -- a penetrating question exposes what was hidden underneath. Incisive adds precision and economy: an incisive analysis is deep and also sharply exact, said cleanly in a few well-chosen words. Penetrating goes deep; incisive goes deep and cuts clean.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

vague: unclear or imprecise

unclear: not easy to understand; lacking precision

Where it sits · how deeply the insight penetrates

clear → incisive → brilliant

clear vs. incisive: A clear explanation is simply easy to understand, but it doesn't necessarily show the sharp, penetrating quality of an incisive one.

brilliant vs. incisive: A brilliant insight is dazzlingly sharp and original, going even further than a merely incisive one.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: into (Latin)

root — cis: to cut (Latin caedere)

suffix — -ive: having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Incisive combines in- ('into') + cis (Latin caedere, 'to cut') + -ive ('having the quality of') -- literally 'having the quality of cutting into,' which is exactly what incisive thinking does: it cuts straight into the heart of a problem with precision.

Use the root in a new word: incision: Dr. Ramos checked the incision at Friday's follow-up appointment.

Root Check

Word Choice

Incisive and trenchant both mean sharp, but incisive praises precision and clarity without necessarily being harsh, while trenchant usually carries a biting, critical edge. An incisive question can be kind; a trenchant one usually stings.
